sources.text: A process sleeps in order to wait for a condition to become true, and the chan argument (the wait channel) names the desired condition. sleep_prepare(chan) declares that a process might soon sleep in order to wait for the indicated wait channel; it returns right away. wakeup(chan) is called when the condition named by chan has (or might have) become true; it wakes up all processes that have called sleep_prepare(chan) and then sleep() with the same chan. sleep() returns right away if wakeup(chan) has already been called after the (required) previous call to sleep_prepare(chan); if not, sleep() marks the calling process as SLEEPING (not RUNNABLE) and releases the CPU by context-switching to the scheduler, so that other processes can run. sleep_prepare() and sleep() are called by the same process (typically within a few lines of each other); wakeup() is called by a different process or by an interrupt handler.

sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition. The call records the fact that the process may need to sleep on the indicated chan. If another process (or interrupt) calls wakeup(chan) between the calls to sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup() sets a flag in the about-to-sleep process indicating that it shouldn’t actually sleep. If sleep() sees this flag, it returns rather than sleeping.

What is the reason for sleep_prepare(chan)? There is the possibility that the condition might become true, and wakeup() called, between when the pipe reader sees that the buffer is empty, and when it calls sleep. Without some cleverness, the wakeup() would not find any sleeping processes, and would not have any effect. Then the process would call sleep() even though the pipe buffer has data to read; and if (as could be the case) the pipe writer never wrote anything more, the reader could incorrectly sleep forever. This undesirable situation is called a lost wake-up. The behavior described in the previous paragraph avoids this problem.

In the pipe example, as in most sleeping code, there is a lock that protects the condition and prevents wakeup() from being called between when the going-to-sleep process checks the condition and when it calls sleep_prepare(). This lock is often called the condition lock. A process must release the lock before calling sleep() (so that some other process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup()), and re-acquire the lock after sleep() returns.

Xv6’s sleep_prepare and sleep and wakeup implement the interface used in the example above. The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for processes sleeping on the given wait channel and marks them RUNNABLE.

sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() changes the calling process to state SLEEPING and calls sched() to let other processes run.

wakeup(chan) handles two situations with respect to some other process that might concurrently be in the process of going to sleep on chan. If that other process has gotten as far as marking itself as SLEEPING, then wakeup will see it in that state and change it to RUNNABLE; its call to sleep() will then return. If the other process has gotten as far as calling sleep_prepare(chan) (but its sleep() has not gotten as far as acquiring p->lock), wakeup(chan) will see that p->chan is equal to chan, and wakeup will set p->chan to zero. In that case, when the other process does call sleep, it will see the zero and return immediately. The point is to avoid a lost wakeup if wakeup() is called just as another process is about to call sleep().

The rules for use of sleep_prepare() prevent us from having to worry about the situation in which an about-to-sleep process hasn’t yet called sleep_prepare(). Either that process surrounds its condition check and sleep_prepare() with a lock that prevents any call to wakeup() for the relevant channel, or that process must call sleep_prepare() before checking the condition.

questions.stem:
A pipe reader executes the following protocol, with condition "buffer nonempty", condition variable `buf_cond`, and condition lock `buf_lock`:

1. acquire(buf_lock)
2. while (buffer empty) {
3.     release(buf_lock)
4.     sleep_prepare(buf_cond)
5.     acquire(buf_lock)
6.     if (buffer empty) sleep(buf_cond)
7.     release(buf_lock)
8. }
9. consume one byte
10. release(buf_lock)

Assume `wakeup(buf_cond)` is called exactly once by a writer immediately after it appends a byte and releases `buf_lock`. `sleep_prepare(chan)`, `sleep(chan)`, and `wakeup(chan)` are defined as in the supplied material: `sleep_prepare(chan)` records `p->chan = chan` and returns; `sleep(chan)` checks whether `p->chan` is still `chan`, and if so marks the process `SLEEPING` and calls `sched()`; if `p->chan` is zero it returns without sleeping. `wakeup(chan)` sets `p->chan = 0` for any process with `p->chan == chan` not yet `SLEEPING`, and marks `RUNNABLE` any process already `SLEEPING` on that channel. All operations are atomic where the material states so; no other wakeups occur.

Which statement best evaluates this protocol?

A. It correctly prevents lost wakeups because it calls `sleep_prepare` while holding `buf_lock`.

B. It can still lose a wakeup, because after a writer appends a byte and calls `wakeup` between lines 3 and 4, the reader then calls `sleep_prepare` after the wakeup and may sleep forever.

C. It correctly prevents lost wakeups because the second check at line 6 occurs after reacquiring `buf_lock`, so the reader will observe any byte appended before `sleep` is called.

D. It can still lose a wakeup, because `wakeup` only wakes processes already `SLEEPING` and ignores the `p->chan` flag set by `sleep_prepare`.
options: It correctly prevents lost wakeups because it calls `sleep_prepare` while holding `buf_lock`.
It can still lose a wakeup, because after a writer appends a byte and calls `wakeup` between lines 3 and 4, the reader then calls `sleep_prepare` after the wakeup and may sleep forever.
It correctly prevents lost wakeups because the second check at line 6 occurs after reacquiring `buf_lock`, so the reader will observe any byte appended before `sleep` is called.
It can still lose a wakeup, because `wakeup` only wakes processes already `SLEEPING` and ignores the `p->chan` flag set by `sleep_prepare`.
questions.explanation: Line 3 releases `buf_lock` before line 4 calls `sleep_prepare`. If a writer acquires `buf_lock`, appends a byte, calls `wakeup(buf_cond)`, and releases `buf_lock` between lines 3 and 4, then when the reader reaches line 4 it calls `sleep_prepare(buf_cond)` after that wakeup. Later, line 6 may find the buffer nonempty and skip `sleep`, or it may find the buffer empty and call `sleep(buf_cond)` with no pending wakeup, causing an indefinite sleep. Option A is false because holding `buf_lock` only during `sleep_prepare` is insufficient if the release happened before `sleep_prepare`; the material requires `sleep_prepare` before releasing the lock. Option C is false because the second check at line 6 can occur after the writer's wakeup was already lost, so rechecking does not guarantee a wakeup is still pending. Option D is false because `wakeup` does handle the `p->chan` flag for a process that has called `sleep_prepare` but not yet slept: it sets `p->chan = 0` so the later `sleep` returns immediately.
questions.difficulty_reason: The student must trace a concrete interleaving in which `sleep_prepare` is called after the wakeup, connect that to the lost-wakeup rule, and distinguish it from superficially similar but insufficient lock or recheck conditions.

expected_steps: Identify that line 3 releases `buf_lock` before line 4 calls `sleep_prepare`.
Construct the interleaving where a writer appends and calls `wakeup(buf_cond)` between lines 3 and 4.
Explain why the later `sleep_prepare(buf_cond)` does not observe that wakeup and why line 6 may still call `sleep` with no pending wakeup, causing an indefinite sleep.
Reject the alternatives by noting that holding the lock only at `sleep_prepare`, rechecking under the lock, or claiming `wakeup` ignores `p->chan` do not prevent the lost wakeup.

Here, the reader releases buf_lock at line 3 before calling sleep_prepare at line 4. A writer can append a byte and call wakeup between lines 3 and 4; at that time no process has p->chan equal to buf_cond, so the wakeup has no effect. A pipe reader executes the following protocol, with condition "buffer nonempty", condition variable `buf_cond`, and condition lock `buf_lock`:

1. acquire(buf_lock)
2. while (buffer empty) {
3.     release(buf_lock)
4.     sleep_prepare(buf_cond)
5.     acquire(buf_lock)
6.     if (buffer empty) sleep(buf_cond)
7.     release(buf_lock)
8. }
9. consume one byte
10. release(buf_lock)

Assume `wakeup(buf_cond)` is called exactly once by a writer immediately after it appends a byte and releases `buf_lock`. `sleep_prepare(chan)`, `sleep(chan)`, and `wakeup(chan)` are defined as in the supplied material: `sleep_prepare(chan)` records `p->chan = chan` and returns; `sleep(chan)` checks whether `p->chan` is still `chan`, and if so marks the process `SLEEPING` and calls `sched()`; if `p->chan` is zero it returns without sleeping. `wakeup(chan)` sets `p->chan = 0` for any process with `p->chan == chan` not yet `SLEEPING`, and marks `RUNNABLE` any process already `SLEEPING` on that channel. All operations are atomic where the material states so; no other wakeups occur.

Which statement best evaluates this protocol?

A. It correctly prevents lost wakeups because it calls `sleep_prepare` while holding `buf_lock`.

B. It can still lose a wakeup, because after a writer appends a byte and calls `wakeup` between lines 3 and 4, the reader then calls `sleep_prepare` after the wakeup and may sleep forever.

C. It correctly prevents lost wakeups because the second check at line 6 occurs after reacquiring `buf_lock`, so the reader will observe any byte appended before `sleep` is called.

D. It can still lose a wakeup, because `wakeup` only wakes processes already `SLEEPING` and ignores the `p->chan` flag set by `sleep_prepare`.

If a writer acquires `buf_lock`, appends a byte, calls `wakeup(buf_cond)`, and releases `buf_lock` between lines 3 and 4, then when the reader reaches line 4 it calls `sleep_prepare(buf_cond)` after that wakeup. Later, line 6 may find the buffer nonempty and skip `sleep`, or it may find the buffer empty and call `sleep(buf_cond)` with no pending wakeup, causing an indefinite sleep. Option A is false because holding `buf_lock` only during `sleep_prepare` is insufficient if the release happened before `sleep_prepare`; the material requires `sleep_prepare` before releasing the lock. Option C is false because the second check at line 6 can occur after the writer's wakeup was already lost, so rechecking does not guarantee a wakeup is still pending. Option D is false because `wakeup` does handle the `p->chan` flag for a process that has called `sleep_prepare` but not yet slept: it sets `p->chan = 0` so the later `sleep` returns immediately.

questions.stem:
A pipe-like buffer is shared by one producer and one consumer using the xv6 sleep_prepare/sleep/wakeup interface. The consumer's intended wait loop is:

1. acquire(condlock)
2. while buffer is empty do:
3.   sleep_prepare(&buf)
4.   release(condlock)
5.   sleep(&buf)
6.   acquire(condlock)
7. end while
8. x = take one item
9. release(condlock)

The producer runs on another CPU and does:

P1. acquire(condlock)
P2. put one item into buffer
P3. wakeup(&buf)
P4. release(condlock)

An engineer proposes replacing the consumer's loop with the supposedly equivalent "flag" version:

F1. acquire(condlock)
F2. while buffer is empty do:
F3.   released = 0
F4.   sleep_prepare(&buf)
F5.   release(condlock)
F6.   if (released == 0) sleep(&buf)
F7.   acquire(condlock)
F8.   if (released == 1) continue
F9. end while
F10. x = take one item
F11. release(condlock)

For every numeric condition, claim, or symbol below, state whether it holds under ordinary xv6 semantics as described in the interface.

Condition 1: In the consumer's original loop, sleep_prepare(&buf) at line 3 must be called before the condition check at line 2 or before releasing the lock at line 4, as required by the interface rules.
Condition 2: In the original loop, if wakeup(&buf) runs between lines 3 and 5, the wakeup sets a flag in the sleeping process so sleep() at line 5 returns without sleeping.
Condition 3: In the original loop, the condition lock at line 1 is what prevents wakeup(&buf) from occurring between the condition check and sleep_prepare(&buf).
Condition 4: In the flag version, the flag 'released' must be set by wakeup() from the producer side before the consumer reads it at line F6.
Condition 5: In the flag version, F8's continue branch rechecks the while condition at line F2 but does not necessarily prevent a lost wakeup if the condition check at F2 is not itself inside a lock.
Condition 6: In the original loop, after sleep() returns and lock is reacquired at line 6, rechecking the while condition at line 2 is required before proceeding to take an item at line 8.

Question: Which option correctly classifies all six conditions under the interface's rules, and identifies the exact failure of the flag version?
options: Condition 1 holds; Condition 2 holds; Condition 3 holds; Condition 4 false because wakeup does not set 'released'; Condition 5 holds only when the condition check is outside any condition lock; Condition 6 holds. The flag version fails because 'released' is not written by wakeup and the sleep is not protected on the condition check side.

Condition 1 holds; Condition 2 false because wakeup never sets a flag; Condition 3 holds; Condition 4 holds; Condition 5 false because continue always prevents lost wakeups; Condition 6 holds. The flag version is correct as written.

Condition 1 holds; Condition 2 holds; Condition 3 holds; Condition 4 holds because wakeup will set the flag; Condition 5 false because the flag version rechecks the condition; Condition 6 holds. The flag version is correct because the wakeup path always sets 'released'.

Condition 1 false because sleep_prepare can be called after sleep; Condition 2 holds; Condition 3 false because sleep itself protects the condition; Condition 4 holds; Condition 5 holds; Condition 6 false because the condition need not be rechecked after sleep returns.
questions.explanation: Condition 1 matches the rule that sleep_prepare must be called before checking the condition or before releasing the lock that protects it. Condition 2 matches the described flag behavior: wakeup may set a flag in the about-to-sleep process so sleep returns without sleeping. Condition 3 matches the condition lock's role in preventing wakeup between the check and sleep_prepare. Condition 4 is false because the interface's wakeup sets p->chan to zero or marks the process RUNNABLE; it does not update a user-level 'released' variable. Condition 5 is true: if the while check at F2 is not protected by a lock that blocks wakeup, the same lost-wakeup race can still occur despite the continue. Condition 6 is true: the condition must be rechecked after sleep returns before taking an item. The flag version therefore does not implement the interface's necessary conditions and can still lose a wakeup.

A pipe-like buffer is shared by one producer and one consumer using the xv6 sleep_prepare/sleep/wakeup interface. The consumer's intended wait loop is:

1. acquire(condlock)
2. while buffer is empty do:
3.   sleep_prepare(&buf)
4.   release(condlock)
5.   sleep(&buf)
6.   acquire(condlock)
7. end while
8. x = take one item
9. release(condlock)

The producer runs on another CPU and does:

P1. acquire(condlock)
P2. put one item into buffer
P3. wakeup(&buf)
P4. release(condlock)

An engineer proposes replacing the consumer's loop with the supposedly equivalent "flag" version:

F1. acquire(condlock)
F2. while buffer is empty do:
F3.   released = 0
F4.   sleep_prepare(&buf)
F5.   release(condlock)
F6.   if (released == 0) sleep(&buf)
F7.   acquire(condlock)
F8.   if (released == 1) continue
F9. end while
F10. x = take one item
F11. release(condlock)

For every numeric condition, claim, or symbol below, state whether it holds under ordinary xv6 semantics as described in the interface.

Condition 1: In the consumer's original loop, sleep_prepare(&buf) at line 3 must be called before the condition check at line 2 or before releasing the lock at line 4, as required by the interface rules.
Condition 2: In the original loop, if wakeup(&buf) runs between lines 3 and 5, the wakeup sets a flag in the sleeping process so sleep() at line 5 returns without sleeping.

sources.text: A process sleeps in order to wait for a condition to become true, and the chan argument (the wait channel) names the desired condition. sleep_prepare(chan) declares that a process might soon sleep in order to wait for the indicated wait channel; it returns right away. wakeup(chan) is called when the condition named by chan has (or might have) become true; it wakes up all processes that have called sleep_prepare(chan) and then sleep() with the same chan. sleep() returns right away if wakeup(chan) has already been called after the (required) previous call to sleep_prepare(chan); if not, sleep() marks the calling process as SLEEPING (not RUNNABLE) and releases the CPU by context-switching to the scheduler, so that other processes can run. sleep_prepare() and sleep() are called by the same process (typically within a few lines of each other); wakeup() is called by a different process or by an interrupt handler.

sleep_prepare(chan) must be called either before checking the condition, or before releasing the lock that protects the condition. The call records the fact that the process may need to sleep on the indicated chan. If another process (or interrupt) calls wakeup(chan) between the calls to sleep_prepare(chan) and sleep(), wakeup() sets a flag in the about-to-sleep process indicating that it shouldn’t actually sleep. If sleep() sees this flag, it returns rather than sleeping.

What is the reason for sleep_prepare(chan)? There is the possibility that the condition might become true, and wakeup() called, between when the pipe reader sees that the buffer is empty, and when it calls sleep. Without some cleverness, the wakeup() would not find any sleeping processes, and would not have any effect. Then the process would call sleep() even though the pipe buffer has data to read; and if (as could be the case) the pipe writer never wrote anything more, the reader could incorrectly sleep forever. This undesirable situation is called a lost wake-up. The behavior described in the previous paragraph avoids this problem.

In the pipe example, as in most sleeping code, there is a lock that protects the condition and prevents wakeup() from being called between when the going-to-sleep process checks the condition and when it calls sleep_prepare(). This lock is often called the condition lock. A process must release the lock before calling sleep() (so that some other process or interrupt handler can modify the condition and call wakeup()), and re-acquire the lock after sleep() returns.

Xv6’s sleep_prepare and sleep and wakeup implement the interface used in the example above. The basic idea is to have sleep mark the current process as SLEEPING and then call sched to release the CPU; wakeup looks for processes sleeping on the given wait channel and marks them RUNNABLE.

sleep_prepare(chan) records the wait channel in p->chan and returns. If p->chan is still non-zero when sleep() is called, sleep() changes the calling process to state SLEEPING and calls sched() to let other processes run.

wakeup(chan) handles two situations with respect to some other process that might concurrently be in the process of going to sleep on chan. If that other process has gotten as far as marking itself as SLEEPING, then wakeup will see it in that state and change it to RUNNABLE; its call to sleep() will then return. If the other process has gotten as far as calling sleep_prepare(chan) (but its sleep() has not gotten as far as acquiring p->lock), wakeup(chan) will see that p->chan is equal to chan, and wakeup will set p->chan to zero. In that case, when the other process does call sleep, it will see the zero and return immediately. The point is to avoid a lost wakeup if wakeup() is called just as another process is about to call sleep().

The rules for use of sleep_prepare() prevent us from having to worry about the situation in which an about-to-sleep process hasn’t yet called sleep_prepare(). Either that process surrounds its condition check and sleep_prepare() with a lock that prevents any call to wakeup() for the relevant channel, or that process must call sleep_prepare() before checking the condition.
